title: State v. Jacques
description: Whether the trial court violated the defendant's constitutional right to a second probable cause hearing, abused its discretion by admitting a prior inconsistent statement from a witness with memory loss, and abused its discretion by admitting unreliable jailhouse informant testimony.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the trial court correctly denied a second probable cause hearing, properly admitted Jenkins' statement as a prior inconsistent statement, and reasonably found Vazquez's testimony reliable, asserting no constitutional violations or abuse of discretion.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court violated his constitutional right to a second probable cause hearing, infringed his confrontation clause rights by admitting Jenkins' statement, and abused its discretion by admitting unreliable jailhouse informant testimony.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of conviction, upholding the trial court's decisions on all three issues raised by the defendant.

title: State v. Michael Sharpe
description: Whether the warrantless collection, testing, and storage of the defendant's involuntarily shed DNA, obtained from discarded clothing by police without a warrant, constitutes an unreasonable invasion of privacy under the state and federal constitutions.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the warrantless collection, testing, and storage of the defendant's shed DNA for identification purposes was constitutional and did not violate privacy rights, as society has no reasonable expectation of privacy in discarded DNA.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the warrantless extraction and testing of his DNA from an object lawfully collected by the police constituted an unreasonable invasion of his privacy under article first, § 7, of the Connecticut constitution and the fourth amendment to the United States constitution.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction, ruling that the warrantless collection, testing, and storage of his DNA was constitutional and did not violate his privacy rights.

title: State v. McFarland
description: Whether the thirty-two year interval between the murders and the defendant's arrest violated his due process rights under the Connecticut constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that the prearrest delay was justified by legitimate investigative reasons and did not violate the defendant's due process rights.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the thirty-two year prearrest delay caused actual and substantial prejudice, violating his due process rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the conviction of the defendant, ruling that the prearrest delay did not violate his due process rights.

title: State v. Haynes
description: Whether illegally obtained statements can be used to impeach a defendant's trial testimony if they are merely inconsistent with the testimony, or only if they are directly contradictory.
plaintiff_argument: The state (majority) argues that illegally obtained statements, even if only inconsistent, can be used to impeach a defendant's trial testimony, following federal precedent.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that illegally obtained statements should only be used for impeachment if they are directly contradictory to trial testimony, not merely inconsistent, to uphold state constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, allowing the state to use the defendant's illegally obtained, inconsistent statements for impeachment purposes during trial.

title: State v. King
description: Whether a defendant's waiver of a jury trial is knowing, intelligent, and voluntary when the trial court fails to inform them that a three-judge panel can render a guilty verdict by a majority vote, unlike the unanimous requirement for a jury.
plaintiff_argument: The state implicitly argued that the defendant's jury trial waiver was valid and the trial court's canvass was sufficient, and that the evidence presented was sufficient to support the conviction.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued her jury trial waiver was involuntary and unconstitutional because the trial court failed to explain that a three-judge panel could reach a guilty verdict by a majority vote, unlike a unanimous jury, and that there was insufficient evidence to support her conviction.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the defendant's conviction and remanded the case for a new trial, ruling that the trial court's canvass for waiving a jury trial was insufficient due to its failure to inform the defendant about the non-unanimous verdict of a three-judge panel.

title: Spillane v. Lamont
description: Whether the doctrine of sovereign immunity bars a declaratory judgment action challenging the constitutionality of P.A. 21-6, which eliminated religious exemptions for school vaccination requirements, and whether a statutory waiver of immunity applies to such challenges.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that P.A. 21-6 violates their constitutional rights to free exercise of religion, equal protection, and free public education, and that sovereign immunity should not bar their challenge.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that sovereign immunity bars the suit, that the plaintiffs' constitutional claims are not substantial enough to overcome immunity, and that the statutory waiver of immunity does not apply to challenges to legislation like P.A. 21-6.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's denial of the defendants' motion to dismiss for the plaintiffs' constitutional claims (counts two through six), concluding these claims are barred by sovereign immunity. The court affirmed the trial court's denial of dismissal for the plaintiffs' statutory free exercise claim (count one), allowing it to proceed.

title: Tatum v. Commissioner of Corrections
description: Whether the principles set forth in Guilbert and Dickson regarding eyewitness identification apply retroactively to the petitioner's case on collateral review.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioner argued that both Guilbert and Dickson announced watershed rules of criminal procedure that should apply retroactively, or alternatively, that justice requires their retroactive application to his case because they overruled specific holdings in his direct appeal.
defendant_argument: The respondent contended that neither Guilbert nor Dickson applies retroactively, citing a footnote in Dickson that stated the new constitutional rule did not apply retroactively on collateral review.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Court's judgment, ruling that the principles of Dickson (regarding unduly suggestive in-court identifications) apply retroactively to the petitioner's case, but Guilbert (regarding expert testimony on eyewitness identification) does not. The case is remanded for a new trial on the relevant counts.

title: State v. Avoletta
description: Whether a special act of the legislature (S.A. 17-4) that permitted the refiling of a previously dismissed claim is an unconstitutional public emolument, with the plaintiff arguing it is unconstitutional as it lacks a legitimate public purpose and the defendant arguing it is constitutional as it serves multiple public policy purposes.
plaintiff_argument: The State of Connecticut argued that S.A. 17-4 is an unconstitutional public emolument because it provides an exclusive, private benefit to the defendants without serving a legitimate public purpose, as the state was not responsible for the defendants' procedural default in filing their claim.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that S.A. 17-4 is not an unconstitutional public emolument because it serves legitimate public policy purposes, including providing compensation for injuries, ensuring safe schools, holding government officials accountable, and allowing full adjudication of similar claims.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the Appellate Court's judgment, concluding that S.A. 17-4 is an unconstitutional public emolument because it does not serve a legitimate public purpose.

title: State v. Langston
description: Whether a trial court can properly consider conduct related to a charge of which a criminal defendant was acquitted, when sentencing the defendant on other charges of which the defendant was convicted.
plaintiff_argument: The sentencing court's consideration of conduct related to a charge of which he was acquitted violated his rights to due process and a trial by jury under both federal and state constitutions.
defendant_argument: The practice of considering acquitted conduct during sentencing is permissible under established federal and state precedent, and the sentence imposed was within the statutorily prescribed range for the counts of conviction.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the trial court's denial of the defendant's motion to correct an illegal sentence.

title: State v. Qinxuan Pan
description: Whether the trial court abused its discretion in setting a $20 million bond and incorrectly denying the defendant's request for a 10 percent cash bail option.
plaintiff_argument: The defendant argued that the $20 million bond was unreasonably high and a functional denial of bail, and that the trial court incorrectly concluded it lacked the authority to grant a 10 percent cash option.
defendant_argument: The state contended that the $20 million bond was reasonable given the defendant's extreme flight risk and public safety concerns, and did not challenge the trial court's conclusion regarding the 10 percent cash option.
decision_outcome: The court upheld the $20 million bond amount as a reasonable exercise of discretion but found that the trial court incorrectly determined it lacked discretion to consider a 10 percent cash bail option, remanding the case for that consideration.

title: State v. Graham
description: Whether the trial court erred in admitting an accomplice's statement and whether the prosecutor's closing arguments constituted impropriety, thereby violating the defendant's confrontation rights and right to a fair trial.
plaintiff_argument: The State argued that the accomplice's statement was admissible as a statement against penal interest and was non-testimonial, thus not violating confrontation rights. It also contended that the prosecutor's tailoring arguments were specific and permissible, and claims regarding cooperation agreements were unpreserved evidentiary claims, not prosecutorial impropriety.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court improperly admitted the accomplice's statement, violating hearsay rules and his confrontation rights. He also claimed the prosecutor's generic tailoring arguments and use of cooperation agreements constituted impropriety and violated his constitutional rights.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of conviction against the defendant.

title: In re Annessa J.
description: Whether the virtual termination of parental rights trial violated the respondent mother's constitutional rights to an in-person trial and confrontation, and whether the Appellate Court correctly expanded the legal standard for posttermination visitation.
plaintiff_argument: The virtual trial did not violate Valerie's constitutional rights, and the Appellate Court improperly expanded the standard for posttermination visitation beyond "necessary or appropriate" to secure the child's welfare.
defendant_argument: Valerie argued the virtual trial violated her state constitutional right to an in-person trial and her federal due process right to confront witnesses. Both respondents argued the trial court applied an incorrect legal standard for posttermination visitation, and the Appellate Court correctly broadened it to include the child's "best interest."
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the termination of parental rights, finding no constitutional violation in the virtual trial, and reversed the Appellate Court's expansion of the standard for posttermination visitation, reinstating the "necessary or appropriate" standard.

title: State v. Morel-Vargas
description: Whether a criminal defendant's waiver of the right to testify must be personally asserted on the record, with the defendant arguing for a personal, on-the-record waiver and the state arguing that defense counsel's representation combined with the defendant's silence is sufficient.
plaintiff_argument: The constitution does not require a defendant to personally assert the waiver of his right to testify on the record; defense counsel's in-court representation, coupled with the defendant's coincident silence, is sufficient for a valid waiver.
defendant_argument: The constitution requires a criminal defendant to affirmatively inform the trial court, either orally or in writing, of his decision to waive his right to testify, and therefore, his counsel's purported waiver was invalid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's conviction, concluding that defense counsel's in-court representation and the defendant's silence constituted a valid constitutional waiver, but prospectively mandated that trial courts either canvass defendants or inquire of defense counsel regarding the waiver of the right to testify.

title: State v. Correa
description: Whether Article first, § 7, of the Connecticut constitution prohibits the police from conducting a warrantless canine sniff of the exterior door to a motel room and a warrantless visual sweep of the room for the purpose of detecting illegal drugs.
plaintiff_argument: The state argued that a warrantless canine sniff of a motel room door is not a search under the state constitution, or if it is, it only requires reasonable articulable suspicion, and that the visual sweep was justified by exigent circumstances or the independent source doctrine.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that a warrantless canine sniff of the motel room door and a warrantless visual sweep of the room violated his rights under Article first, § 7, of the Connecticut constitution, requiring a warrant based on probable cause.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Appellate Court's judgment, concluding that a warrantless canine sniff of a motel room door is an unlawful search requiring a warrant and that the visual sweep was not justified by exigent circumstances, remanding the case for the state to present evidence on independent source and inevitable discovery doctrines.

title: State v. Bemer
description: Whether the trial court's order for sexually transmitted disease and HIV testing of the defendant, based solely on being charged with a sexual offense, violates the defendant's constitutional right to be free from unreasonable searches, with the plaintiff arguing the statute broadly authorizes such testing and the defendant arguing it requires a finding of clear and imminent danger or compelling need.
plaintiff_argument: The state and victims argued that General Statutes § 54-102a (b) broadly authorizes HIV testing when a defendant is charged with an enumerated sexual offense, without requiring the stringent 'clear and imminent danger' or 'compelling need' standard from § 19a-582 (d) (8), and that the statute is constitutional.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the trial court abused its discretion by ordering HIV testing without a finding of 'clear and imminent danger' and 'compelling need' as required by General Statutes § 19a-582 (d) (8), which he contended is incorporated into § 54-102a (b), and that the statute otherwise violates his state constitutional rights against unreasonable searches.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the trial court's order for sexually transmitted disease examination and HIV testing and remanded the case for a new hearing, requiring the trial court to find that such testing would provide useful, practical information to a victim that cannot reasonably be obtained otherwise.

title: Anthony A. v. Commissioner of Corrections
description: Whether the Department of Correction violated the petitioner's constitutional rights to procedural and substantive due process by classifying him as a sex offender based on non-conviction information and the procedures used.
plaintiff_argument: The Department of Correction violated his procedural due process rights by denying him the opportunity to call witnesses, providing inadequate notice of evidence, and using partial decision-makers, and violated his substantive due process rights by classifying him as a sex offender without conviction, which constituted unwarranted punishment.
defendant_argument: The Department of Correction afforded the petitioner all necessary due process, the classification was supported by sufficient evidence, and it did not violate substantive due process or constitute unwarranted punishment.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the habeas court's judgment, finding that the Department of Correction violated the petitioner's procedural due process rights under both federal and state constitutions, and directed the expungement of his sex treatment need score.

title: Fay v. Merrill
description: Whether Governor Ned Lamont's Executive Order No. 7QQ, which added COVID-19 as a permissible reason for absentee voting, violates article sixth, § 7, of the Connecticut constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Governor lacked the constitutional authority to expand absentee voting reasons, as this power is reserved for the General Assembly, and that "sickness" in the constitution does not encompass a pandemic without regard to individual voter circumstances.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the legislature's ratification of Executive Order No. 7QQ rendered the separation of powers claim moot, and that the constitutional term "sickness" broadly encompasses a pandemic like COVID-19, not just an individual's personal illness.
decision_outcome: The court dismissed the plaintiffs' separation of powers claim as moot due to legislative ratification and affirmed the trial court's judgment, ruling that Executive Order No. 7QQ does not violate article sixth, § 7, of the Connecticut constitution.
